blocks.text: The chapter treats Spirit-given gifts as diverse but ordered toward common benefit and mutual dependence. Its central concern is not identifying one superior experience, but explaining how differentiated members belong and serve together.

Verses 4–11 coordinate varieties of gifts, services, and activities with the same Spirit, Lord, and God. The examples that follow are therefore framed by verse 7: a manifestation is given for shared benefit, rather than as a personal entitlement or a measure of spiritual rank.

The body image joins one Spirit and one body with real social and functional difference: Jews and Greeks, enslaved and free, and members with different roles all belong. The analogy resists letting a single manifestation, office, class, ethnicity, or embodiment define the whole community; difference is not exclusion from the body.

The argument becomes sharper in verses 21–26: members thought weaker are necessary, and those treated as less honorable receive greater honor and care. The later list of apostles, prophets, teachers, helps, and other functions should therefore not erase ordinary service or be treated as a complete hierarchy of human worth.

The opening confession makes allegiance to Jesus more basic than spiritual spectacle, and the closing rhetorical questions expect differentiated answers: not everyone has the same role or gift. In that setting, the repeated plural wording for “gifts of healings” belongs among diverse distributions rather than guaranteeing that every person will exercise the same function.

“Kinds of tongues” and “interpretation of tongues” are named together, but the exact nature of tongues is uncertain. The passage identifies them as Spirit-related speech requiring interpretation in the assembly without settling every later question about their form.

The chapter supplies a communal measure for authority claims: shared benefit matters more than charisma, office, performance, or a claimed revelation. Its concern for members receiving less honor also keeps communal participation and care in view rather than treating visible intensity as the standard of value.

Later Christians disagree about whether and how gifts such as tongues, prophecy, healings, miracles, and apostles continue. This paragraph itself should not be made to settle that wider dispute without qualification. It also distinguishes gifts, services, activities, roles, speech, discernment, and healing rather than making any one of them a compulsory test of belonging or rank.

Verse 31 leads directly into chapter 13, where extraordinary speech, knowledge, faith, giving, and sacrifice are declared worthless without love. In this literary setting, love is not detached romantic sentiment: its patience, kindness, truthfulness, and refusal to insist on its own way address rivalry and self-display in the discussion of gifts.

Acts depicts recognizable diaspora languages at Pentecost, but how that depiction relates to other early Christian speech phenomena remains debated. That comparison should therefore not be used to define the tongues of this passage more precisely than the passage itself does.
